components.name: prefix
components.description: Leading text of the secret field's documented example value (mdb_sa_sk_ followed by an ellipsis). Only the example documents it; no page states that every secret begins this way.

components.name: body
components.description: Characters after the prefix. Their alphabet and length are not documented in any page read.

components.name: client-id
components.description: The Client ID of the same service account: mdb_sa_id_ followed by 24 hexadecimal characters, documented as a schema pattern. It is the username-like half of the pair, not the secret.

claims.statement: Each Atlas service account has a client ID and a rotatable secret that function as a username and a password for creating access tokens through the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow.

sources.supports: Each service account has a client ID and a rotatable secret that function as a username and a password for creating access tokens.

claims.statement: The full service account secret is returned only in the response that creates it; later reads return a masked value.

sources.supports: ServiceAccountSecret.secret: 'The secret for the Service Account. It will be returned only the first time after creation.'; maskedSecretValue: 'The masked Service Account secret.'
'This is the only time you can view the full client secret.'

claims.statement: The Atlas Administration API specification gives an example value for the secret and for its masked form that begins with the text mdb_sa_sk_ followed by an ellipsis; it states neither a body alphabet nor a length.

sources.supports: ServiceAccountSecret.secret and maskedSecretValue both carry the example 'mdb_sa_sk_...'

claims.statement: The service account Client ID is specified as mdb_sa_id_ followed by 24 hexadecimal characters of either case (pattern ^mdb_sa_id_[a-fA-F\d]{24}$).
A service account secret has an expiration set when it is created (secretExpiresAfterHours, whose bounds the organization controls) and the documentation describes the secret as rotatable.

sources.supports: secretExpiresAfterHours: 'The minimum and maximum allowed expiration times are subject to change and are controlled by the organization's settings.'

claims.statement: The documented way to use the client ID and secret is an HTTP Basic Authorization header carrying the base64 of CLIENT_ID:CLIENT_SECRET, posted to https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/oauth/token with grant_type=client_credentials.

sources.supports: info.description curl example: Authorization: Basic base64(CLIENT_ID:CLIENT_SECRET), grant_type=client_credentials, token endpoint https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/oauth/token

claims.statement: MongoDB describes service accounts as the recommended authentication method for the Atlas Administration API and programmatic API keys as a legacy option.

sources.supports: info.description: 'Service accounts are the recommended authentication method and API keys are considered a legacy option.'
'Service accounts are the recommended method to manage authentication'

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed. Not researched beyond the pages named in the claims (read 2026-10-04). The prefix rests on one schema example; it is recorded as a documented example, not as a promise.

openQuestions.question: What alphabet and length does the part of the secret after mdb_sa_sk_ have, and is the prefix present on every secret? The pages read give only a truncated example. Settling it needs a provider statement or an issued credential, which desk research cannot obtain.
Does the secret carry a checksum or version segment? No page read mentions one.
Were service account secrets issued with a different format before the mdb_sa_ prefix scheme? The pages read give no history and no archive snapshot was available.
